name: Treaty with the Umpqua and Kalapuya, 1854
aka: Treaty with the Umpqua and Calapooia of the Umpqua Valley, November 29, 1854
nations: Kalapuya (Calapooia) of the Umpqua Valley, including the Yoncalla
promises: Article 1: a reservation on the Umpqua River near Cole's Valley "held by said confederated bands" as an Indian reservation.

Article 1: if the President moved them elsewhere, a delegation of three or more of their principal men had to concur in choosing the new reserve, and the tracts they occupied were to be sold and the money spent on improvements on the new reserve for the holders.
Article 3: annuities for twenty years: $3,000 a year for five years, then $2,300, $1,700 and $1,000 a year for five years each.
In return the bands ceded their country in the Umpqua Valley between the Calapooia Mountains and the Cow Creek and Galice Creek purchases.

breaches.what: The Court of Claims held that the Umpqua and Calapooia bands never gave up the part of the reserve kept by Article 1 that they occupied, that their removal did not take away their treaty rights in it, and that they were entitled to its value from their removal on December 21, 1855, with interest.

breaches.what: The same opinion held that the Act of March 3, 1875, which made Indians work for annuities already owed, was 'a plain violation' of the treaties, and that appropriated treaty funds went unspent. Under this treaty it allowed $1,198.19 for the work order and $13,117.69 for unspent funds and administrative expense.

compensation: The annuities in Article 3. In 1950 the Court of Claims valued the reservation at $67,820 on December 21, 1855, added $309,357.16 as interest to make just compensation and the $14,315.88 it had allowed in 1946, deducted $48,028.30 in gratuities and $1,014 diverted from the Siletz Indians, and entered judgment of $342,450.74 for the Umpqua and Calapooia Indians of the Umpqua Valley, with 4 percent a year on $67,820 from April 3, 1950 until paid.
today: The Court of Claims found in 1946 that these bands were confederated with the Molalla by the treaty of December 21, 1855 and soon after placed on the Grand Ronde Reservation, where they still lived. The Western Oregon termination act of August 13, 1954 (68 Stat. 724) named the Upper Umpqua, Calapooya and Yoncalla among the tribes whose federal supervision was to end. The Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde are the successors.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribes list this treaty among the ratified and unratified treaties of the 1850s that ceded land from the Coast Range to the Cascades and resulted in the forced removal of tribal members from their homelands.

openQuestions: Whether the twenty years of annuities were paid in full was not researched.
The Grand Ronde treaties page names the Upper Umpqua and Yoncalla for this treaty; the treaty text calls the parties the Umpqua and the Calapooias of the Umpqua Valley.

Audit 2026-11-08: both Rogue River Tribe opinions were read in full from the Caselaw Access Project. They hold that the bands kept their rights in the occupied part of the Article 1 reserve, value its taking on December 21, 1855, find the 1875 work order a violation of the treaties and allow unspent treaty funds. Added as three court-ruling breaches; the status rises from no-breach-found to broken on this evidence.

Whether a delegation concurred in choosing Grand Ronde, and whether the reserve tracts were sold for the holders under Article 1, is not discussed in the opinions; the 1946 court deducted any sale proceeds spent for them from the land award.
A 1950 petition by the United States for certiorari (No. 282) appears in catalogue records; its outcome and whether the $342,450.74 was paid were not traced.

plain.promised: The Umpqua and Kalapuya of the Umpqua Valley gave up their country for a reservation on the Umpqua River, twenty years of annuities, and a say in choosing any new reserve if moved.
plain.happened: The Court of Claims held in 1946 that the bands kept their rights in the reserve they were removed from in 1855, and that an 1875 law making them work for promised annuities violated the treaty.
plain.today: In 1950 the court valued the reserve, about 67,820 acres, at $67,820 and entered judgment for $342,450.74 after interest and offsets. Congress ended federal services to these peoples in 1954.

landTaken: The Court of Claims found the Article 1 reservation contained approximately 67,820 acres in the Umpqua Valley, Douglas County, Oregon, taken on December 21, 1855 (89 F. Supp. 798, finding 3).
